q: Why does Terraform need a state file? (select all)
options: To map resource addresses in config to real object IDs
To remember dependencies so it can destroy in the right order after blocks are deleted
To store the provider binaries
To know that a resource removed from config must be destroyed
explain: State maps addresses to IDs, records dependencies and attributes, and is the only record of objects whose blocks were deleted. Provider binaries live in `.terraform/providers`.

q: Which S3 backend setting is the current recommended way to lock state?
options: `dynamodb_table = "terraform-locks"`
`lock = true`
`use_lockfile = true`
`encrypt = true`
explain: `use_lockfile = true` uses S3 conditional writes to create a `.tflock` object next to the state (GA since Terraform 1.11). `dynamodb_table` still works but is deprecated. `encrypt` is about server-side encryption, not locking.

q: A hotfix changed a container's restart policy by hand, and the team agrees the new value is correct. What is the right sequence?
options: Update the `.tf` code to the new value, then apply (optionally `apply -refresh-only` first to record it)
Run `terraform apply`; it will keep the manual value
Edit `terraform.tfstate` by hand to the new value
Run `terraform state rm` and re-import
explain: Accepting drift means changing code. A normal apply without code changes would revert the hotfix. `-refresh-only` records observed values in state but doesn't change your config, so the next plan would revert it unless the code is updated.

q: You renamed `resource "aws_db_instance" "main"` to `"primary"`. The plan shows `1 to add, 1 to destroy`. What should you do?
options: Apply; Terraform will copy the data
Add `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` and apply
Use `-replace=aws_db_instance.primary`
Add `moved { from = aws_db_instance.main  to = aws_db_instance.primary }` and re-plan
explain: A `moved` block tells Terraform the old and new addresses are the same object, so the plan becomes a no-op move. `prevent_destroy` would just make the plan fail; `-replace` forces exactly the destruction you want to avoid.

q: `terraform plan` fails with `Error acquiring the state lock`. The lock info shows your colleague's laptop, created 3 hours ago, and they confirm their laptop crashed mid-apply. What do you do?
options: Run `terraform apply -lock=false`
Delete the state file and re-import everything
Run `terraform force-unlock <lock ID>`, then plan carefully to see what the interrupted apply left behind
Wait; locks expire automatically after 24 hours
explain: Once you've confirmed nobody is running Terraform, `force-unlock` with the ID from the error releases the stale lock. Then a plan shows whatever partial state the crashed apply left. `-lock=false` risks corruption, and S3 lockfiles don't expire.

q: Why can't a backend block reference `var.environment`?
options: Backends are configured during `init`, before variables are evaluated
Variables are always sensitive
It's allowed in Terraform 1.10+
Backend blocks can only contain numbers
explain: The backend must be initialised before Terraform can load state and evaluate the rest of the configuration. Use partial configuration: `backend "s3" {}` plus `terraform init -backend-config=prod.s3.tfbackend`.

q: An S3 bucket was created by hand years ago. You want Terraform to manage it without recreating it. What's the recommended approach?
options: Write the resource block and apply; Terraform will detect the existing bucket
Use a `data` source; that makes Terraform manage it
Add an `import` block with `to` and `id`, generate or write matching config, and apply when the plan shows `1 to import` and no destructive changes
Use a `moved` block from the bucket name
explain: `import` blocks (1.5+) adopt existing objects through a reviewable plan. `terraform plan -generate-config-out=file.tf` can draft the config. A plain resource block would try to create a new bucket and fail; data sources only read.

q: You want Terraform to stop managing a container (another team will own it) without deleting it. Which is the config-driven way?
options: `removed { from = docker_container.x  lifecycle { destroy = false } }`
Delete the resource block
`moved { from = docker_container.x  to = null }`
`lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }`
explain: A `removed` block with `destroy = false` (1.7+) drops the object from state and leaves it running, and shows that in the plan. Deleting the block would destroy the container. The imperative equivalent is `terraform state rm`.

q: Which statements about secrets in state are true? (select all)
options: Values marked `sensitive` are stored in plain text in state
The state bucket should have encryption, versioning and restricted access
`random_password` results end up in state
Using the S3 backend automatically removes secrets from state
explain: Sensitivity only affects display. Anything a provider returns, including generated passwords and keys, is stored in state. Backends store state; they don't strip secrets. Protect the bucket, and prefer designs (ephemeral values, managed secrets) that keep secrets out of state.

q: A container is stuck in a broken state that Terraform can't detect. How do you recreate it through Terraform?
options: `terraform taint` is the only option
`terraform state rm docker_container.web` then apply
`terraform apply -refresh-only`
`terraform apply -replace=docker_container.web`
explain: `-replace` plans a destroy/create of that one resource and shows it in the plan. It supersedes `taint`. `state rm` + apply would create a second container and conflict on the name.

q: `terraform state push restore.tfstate` is rejected. The file's lineage matches the remote state but its serial is lower. What does the check protect against?
options: Pushing a state from a different configuration
Overwriting newer state changes with an older copy by accident
Pushing a state with invalid JSON
Pushing a state from a different Terraform version
explain: The serial increases on every write. A lower serial means your file is older than what's stored. Lineage protects against pushing a completely unrelated state. If you really want the older version, push deliberately (bump the serial or `-force`) after verifying.

q: You moved from local state to an S3 backend by adding a backend block. Which command copies your existing state into the bucket?
options: `terraform init -reconfigure`
`terraform init -migrate-state`
`terraform state push`
`terraform apply -refresh-only`
explain: `init -migrate-state` copies state from the old backend to the new one. `-reconfigure` switches backend config without copying, which you use when pointing at a different, already-populated state.

q: Why do many teams avoid CLI workspaces (`terraform workspace new prod`) for separating environments?
options: All environments share the same code and backend credentials, and the active workspace isn't visible in code, so it's easy to apply to the wrong one
Workspaces don't support remote backends
Workspaces are deprecated
Workspaces can't have different variable values
explain: Workspaces work with S3 (`env:/<name>/key`) and aren't deprecated, but they make environment selection implicit and couple access control. Separate directories or backend config files per environment are more explicit. Workspaces suit short-lived copies like per-branch stacks.
